paras: The killing of Adam Golden occurred on a Monday night in December 1888, when a masked mob stoning the house of Jennie Maddox, seven miles north of Buchanan in Haralson County, Georgia, beat and shot to death Golden, a Black man who had intervened. Five white men and two Black men were jailed for the murder and three white women were held for taking part. The story ran on the telegraph across the country, where it appeared beside reports of White Cap outrages and under headlines such as "Killed for His Interference."

Maddox was described by the Savannah Morning News as "regarded as being a bad character," and by the wire as "a woman of bad repute." According to the Savannah paper, she had incurred the enmity of the women of the neighborhood, and some of their husbands and sons joined them against her.

On Monday night a masked mob of men and women surrounded the Maddox house, stoning it and breaking windows. Golden, whom the Savannah Morning News called "a harmless and well respected colored man," went over and remonstrated. In that account, a man named Reeves said, "Let us kill the — rascal," and Golden threw Reeves in the struggle that followed. Two men then pulled Golden off and struck him on the head with a fence rail, killing him.
The men gathered around and fired their pistols into the body, and the Savannah paper added that they kicked the corpse and "inflicted other indignities."

By December 20 five white men and two Black men were in jail at Buchanan charged with the murder, and three white women were being guarded at their homes. The Savannah Morning News named the jailed men as Bill Reeves, Bud Head, William Ayers, Joe Sanford and a man named Anderson, whose wife and two daughters were also in custody. A week later the same paper reported that Reeves, Head, Ayers and Sandford had waived examination and were held for trial at the June court, that Anderson had a hearing and was bound over, and that the cases against the three women were abandoned. No report of the June trial or its outcome was found in the coverage.

The first report, an Atlanta dispatch of December 20, appeared the next day in the Richmond Dispatch, the Savannah Morning News and, in a news summary, the Wilmington Daily Republican. The Savannah Morning News followed on December 22 with the fullest account, the only one to name the accused, describe the motive against Maddox, and quote Reeves. Its language favored Golden, calling him harmless and "well respected" and calling the treatment of the corpse "indignities."

Outside Georgia the case traveled as a short Atlanta wire, and headline writers gave it different turns. The Clarksville Evening Chronicle and the Maysville Evening Bulletin titled it "Killed for His Interference," while the Grand Rapids Telegram-Herald used "He Will Not Interfere Again." In Dakota, the Jamestown Weekly Alert and the Mitchell Capital ran a variant under "A Lynching Party Needed," a heading aimed at the killers. The Waterbury Evening Democrat placed a separate Atlanta item, which said the young men had "imitated the White Caps," in a column headed "White Cap Outrages Continue."

A one-sentence brief copied in late December by papers in Missouri, Arkansas and Alabama said Golden was killed "while defending a helpless woman from a mob." None of the reports described the killing in racial terms beyond identifying Golden as "colored" and the accused by race.

The weapon differs by report: the first Atlanta wire said someone struck Golden with an axe, the Savannah brief said the crowd shot him and struck him with an ax, and the fuller later accounts said a fence rail, with pistols fired into the body afterward. The White Cap dispatch alone called Golden "a negro employed at the house" and the attackers "half a dozen young men," where other reports described a neighbor and a mob of men and women. The later brief dated the arrests to "the 21st," though the Atlanta dispatch of December 20 already reported the men in jail.

accounts.label: First Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: A crowd of men stoning the house of a woman of bad repute turned on Golden when he asked them to desist, and someone killed him with an axe.

accounts.label: White Cap dispatch
accounts.gist: Half a dozen young men imitating the White Caps attacked the house of 'a woman of easy virtue'; a negro employed there remonstrated and was beaten and shot to death.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News account
accounts.gist: Neighborhood women hostile to Jennie Maddox, joined by husbands and sons, stoned her house as a masked mob; Golden fought Reeves, was brained with a fence rail, and the men fired pistols into his body.

accounts.label: Later Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: A masked mob of men and women stoned the Maddox residence; Golden remonstrated, was brained in the fight, and pistols were fired into the body; five white and two colored men jailed, three white women guarded.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News called Golden 'harmless and well respected' and described the firing into and kicking of the corpse as 'indignities'.
Northern and western papers ran the wire under 'Killed for His Interference' and 'He Will Not Interfere Again', or under 'A Lynching Party Needed'.
The Waterbury Evening Democrat filed the killing in a column of 'White Cap Outrages' from Ohio and Pennsylvania.
A widely copied brief said Golden was killed 'while defending a helpless woman from a mob'.
